items.title: Hubert Laws — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I saw a picture in your photo gallery over there of you and Wynton very close.

ctx.x: Maybe it should have been. Because, here again, the music’s more important than me. That’s the way I think about it. I’m just a participant, but the music’s more important. Maybe it would have been to the advantage to show that the classical and jazz and Latin and all that stuff can contribute to the whole of the jazz performance. In that way it could have helped. That way any aspiring musicians can also involve themselves in different idioms.

For me, like you say, I believe music is a healing force. I saw a picture in your photo gallery over there of you and Wynton very close. Wynton got all the accolades for being able to bridge both worlds, but you – for me, you pioneered that. Like I said, this was the soundtrack to my college years. I was studying music formally. Here I heard, oh,
a jazz musician playing classical and being able to straddle both and do both at such an exceptional, phenomenal level. So that was . . .
